# Component catalogue

Use a component only when it improves comprehension, scanning, decision-making, or task completion.

| Component | Use it for | Avoid when |
|---|---|---|
| Hero / intro | Naming the page and its value | The page is a tiny reference note |
| Lead paragraph | Stating the core point | It merely repeats the heading |
| Step list | Sequential actions | Items are not actually sequential |
| Callout | A distinct warning, prerequisite, or useful tip | Every paragraph is styled as a callout |
| Comparison table | Comparing the same attributes across options | Content is prose or a process |
| Process flow | Showing sequence, roles, or handoffs | A short numbered list is clearer |
| Definition | Explaining a necessary term | The term is already familiar |
| `<details>` disclosure | Optional reference or troubleshooting | Critical information must be visible |
| Checklist | Supporting a repeatable task | It duplicates the steps without added value |
| Knowledge check | Reinforcing a key concept | It is trivia or decorative interaction |
| Code block | Showing exact commands or syntax | A plain-language explanation is enough |

## Component rules

- One visual treatment should have one consistent meaning.
- Label callouts with meaningful text such as "Before you begin" or "Important."
- Keep card content concise; do not put a long article inside a card.
- Use tables with `<caption>`, `<thead>`, and scoped headers when appropriate.
- Ensure interactive components work with keyboard and assistive technology.
- Never hide required actions or critical caveats inside collapsed content.
